doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Attic Victrola and early Latin influences
summary: In the Attleboro house attic he found an Edison Victrola with the Borodin 'Peasant Overture' and Latin records, which gave him an early feel for Latin music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yeah I think I always had that. I remember one of the early people that do interviews asked me, “what are the highlights that you think about,” you know in your whole life of music. And one of them, I mentioned that I was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts. And in our house, there was a basement. My dad practically built the house with his own hands. There was a basement, a first floor which had a kitchen, a front hall, living room and dining room, and then the second floor had the bedrooms and a bathroom, and then above, what we used to call the attic. And that was where you kept all the junk you know, the extra stuff. One day I went up in the attic and I discovered a Victrola we called it. It © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

was an old Edison cylinder type Victrola. And there were some of the old records there. And I discovered first, my first initiation into music really, except for what I told you about my mom and dad playing, was to hear the Borodin “Peasant Overture.” And that was a real charge to me. I couldn’t believe things could be like that musically. And I sat and must have listened to that thing for two hours. And then I started looking at some of the other things and there was a lot of Latin stuff there. And I listened to a lot of Latin stuff, and I think I got a feel for Latin very early on from that. And that stuck with me.
